title: Company-Wise Assessment Profiles
tagline: Year 4 — Building your own one-page profile for each employer from official sources, and comparing profiles quantitatively

introduction.overview: Different employers use different assessments, and they change them. Rather than memorising claims about companies, build your own one-page profile for each employer you are applying to: stages, sections, questions, time, penalty, cutoff stated in official material, and the skills each stage tests. A profile lets you compare employers, plan your preparation time and track what you still need to confirm. This chapter uses hypothetical profiles to teach the comparison; All figures and rules in this chapter's examples are hypothetical teaching examples and are not the rules of any real company or platform; always read the official instructions.
introduction.placementRelevance: Targeted preparation is more efficient than generic preparation once you know what each employer tests.
introduction.realWorldContext: Preparing for an interview by researching the organisation is the same habit.

learningObjectives: List the fields of an assessment profile
Compare two profiles by pace and marks per minute
Update profiles when official information changes

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: A profile records facts from official sources; unverified items are marked "to confirm".

coreDefinitions: Profile: a one-page summary of an assessment.
Stage: one step (aptitude test, technical test, interview).
Weight: the share of total marks of a section.
Unconfirmed: a detail you have not verified.
Source: where a fact comes from.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: A profile turns hearsay into a checklist.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Write fields, fill from official sources, mark gaps, and compute pace and weight.

mainNarrative: Hypothetical profile X: Aptitude 20 questions, 25 minutes; Reasoning 15, 20 minutes; Verbal 25, 20 minutes; 1 mark each. Profile Y: Aptitude 30, 40 minutes; Reasoning 20, 25 minutes; Verbal 20, 15 minutes.
Profile X has 60 questions in 65 minutes (65 ÷ 60 ≈ 1.08 minutes per question); profile Y has 70 in 80 minutes (about 1.14).
Weights in X: Aptitude 20/60 = 33%, Reasoning 25%, Verbal 42%.
If you have 90 hours of preparation and want to follow weights, give Verbal about 37 hours in X.
Mark any field you cannot verify as "to confirm" and ask the recruiter or check the official notice.

deepDiveAspects.title: Profiles go stale
deepDiveAspects.content: Date every profile and re-check before the test.

deepDiveAspects.title: Preparing for the skill, not the company
deepDiveAspects.content: Core skills transfer between employers; use profiles to prioritise, not to narrow.

solvedExamples.title: Weight
solvedExamples.question: Profile X has 60 marks in total and Verbal has 25 marks. Verbal weight?

solvedExamples.title: Allocation
solvedExamples.question: You have 90 hours and Verbal is 41.7% of marks. Hours for Verbal?

solvedExamples.title: Gap list
solvedExamples.question: You do not know whether the test has a penalty. What do you record?
solvedExamples.finalAnswer: "To confirm" and check the official notice

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Fill one page per employer from official sources, compute pace and weights, and list unconfirmed fields.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Eliminate unlikely sections after confirmation only.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: The profile is your checklist, not your prediction.

sourcesAndReferences.sourceName: Official instructions published by each test provider and employer
sourcesAndReferences.referenceNote: Exam patterns and rules change; this chapter teaches how to read and plan around the official instructions and quotes no company-specific figures.
